interactions: Insulin in cirrhosis: reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogen reserve and reduced hepatic insulin clearance prolong insulin action and increase the risk and duration of hypoglycemia; reduce doses and monitor capillary glucose closely

Metoprolol with insulin: beta-blockade can blunt adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (tremor, palpitations) and delay glucose recovery; less marked with cardioselective agents than with non-selective beta-blockers
Lactulose and rifaximin: no clinically relevant interaction with insulin, metoprolol or furosemide
output.proposed: Insulin glargine 22 units nightly and insulin lispro 6 units with meals in Child-Pugh B cirrhosis after insulin-induced hypoglycemia; with metoprolol succinate, furosemide and lactulose
warnings: Give prandial insulin only with a meal actually eaten; omit the dose when intake is poor
Avoid sedative drugs (benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, opioids) in hepatic encephalopathy
Sulfa allergy: furosemide is a non-antibiotic sulfonamide that she already tolerates; avoid sulfonamide antibiotics

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.
Do not stop basal insulin abruptly without a replacement plan: reduce the glargine dose and monitor glucose to avoid rebound hyperglycemia.
required_recommendations: Identify and treat the precipitant: insulin-induced hypoglycemia after a skipped meal; give IV dextrose as needed and monitor capillary glucose every 1-2 hours until stable.

Reduce the glargine dose and give prandial lispro only with meals actually eaten, because cirrhosis impairs gluconeogenesis and insulin clearance; educate the patient and her husband on recognising hypoglycemia and on omitting prandial insulin when she does not eat.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE and ascites, MELD-Na 12 (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD-Na 12), precipitated by insulin-induced hypoglycemia (glucose nadir 42 mg/dL) after a skipped meal; disorientation and asterixis persisting after glucose correction indicate concurrent HE.

differential.key_features: Nadir 42 mg/dL corrected within 30 minutes, too brief for lasting neuroglycopenic injury; asterixis appearing after correction points to a second metabolic process, while diffuse EEG slowing does not separate the two.
Afebrile, WBC 7.4; ascitic PMN 62 cells/mm3, below 250, with no growth.
No focal deficit; non-contrast CT shows no acute abnormality.
SpO2 98% on air, respiratory rate 16, no history of sleep-disordered breathing.
Clear iatrogenic trigger (full insulin doses with a skipped meal); the high insulin level is expected on insulin therapy; no need to pursue insulinoma.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status.

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh B (8: bilirubin 1.8 1, albumin 2.9 2, INR 1.4 1, mild ascites 2, HE grade 2 2); MELD-Na 12 (creatinine 0.8, bilirubin 1.8, INR 1.4, sodium 137)

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance, constipation, sedatives, dehydration, renal failure and, in insulin-treated diabetes, hypoglycemia.
Hypoglycemia in cirrhosis is more frequent and prolonged because hepatic gluconeogenesis and insulin clearance are impaired; insulin regimens must account for liver disease.
Persistent confusion after glucose correction is a key signal that a second process (often HE) is present.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hypoglycemia triggered the presentation, but disorientation and new asterixis persisting after glucose was corrected to 84 mg/dL, in a patient with cirrhosis, indicate concurrent hepatic encephalopathy that needs treatment.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all confusion to hypoglycemia and discharge once glucose normalizes.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Obesity is a NASH risk factor; SpO2 98% and a respiratory rate of 16 give no sign of hypoventilation; the precipitant is hypoglycemia with concurrent HE, not OSA.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue obesity-related causes (OSA, hypercapnia) as primary.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R. is a 44-year-old woman with NASH cirrhosis and insulin-treated type 2 diabetes who was brought to the emergency department by her husband after he found her confused at home while she was preparing dinner. He noted she was speaking incoherently, could not recognize him briefly, and appeared unsteady. She had taken her full basal insulin dose of 22 units the previous evening and her breakfast lispro dose of 6 units at 8 AM but then ate only a small snack rather than a full meal, having felt nauseous and without appetite since yesterday. Her glucose on arrival by EMS was 42 mg/dL, and she received oral glucose gel en route with partial improvement. In the ED, point-of-care glucose was 42 mg/dL and D50W was administered immediately. After glucose correction to 84 mg/dL over 30 minutes, her confusion persisted — she remained disoriented, slow, and had asterixis that appeared on exam 2 hours later.

neurological_exam.additional: Basal-bolus insulin regimen (no insulin pump). Point-of-care glucose on arrival 42 mg/dL; D50W 50 mL given; repeat glucose 68 mg/dL at 15 minutes and 84 mg/dL at 30 minutes. Mental status slightly improved but she remains confused. Mild ascites. No jaundice. No spider angiomata.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal, reactive. Extraocular movements intact. Facial symmetry intact. Gag present.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 14 (E4V4M6). Alert but confused — disoriented to time. Oriented to person and place. Slow to process questions. Asterixis absent on admission — prominent asterixis on arm extension on repeat exam 2 hours later. Number Connection Test 52 seconds (significantly elevated).
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 throughout. No focal deficits. Tone normal on first exam.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ upper extremities, 1+ lower (neuropathy). Plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Decreased sensation bilateral feet — known diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
